introduction: These readings begin by removing a distance: whoever attains the presence of the Manifestation of God has attained the “Presence of God”, and whoever remembers Him far away is “present and visible”. Then they follow the longing, the journeys over land and sea, the days of meeting remembered, the many who desired and were prevented and are told that the desire is counted as attainment, the reunion hoped for beyond death, and the thanks of those who returned. Almost every turn has company. The psalmist thirsts like a hart and would rather keep a door in the house of God; Jacob’s spirit revives at news of Joseph; Simeon’s eyes have seen; the Qur’an says that God is nigh and that His countenance is wherever one turns; Rumi’s reed laments its separation. Other voices stand over against the readings. “There shall no man see me, and live,” Moses is told, and Israel begs not to hear the voice; Isaiah is undone by what he sees; Kabir’s God is beside the seeker and needs no pilgrimage; Thomas hears that those who have not seen are the blessed ones; and the Preacher doubts that the dead meet anyone.
questions: “He that hath seen me hath seen the Father”, and “there shall no man see me, and live”. How do the readings of the first two parts hold both sayings together?

The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of God; Kabir’s God says “I am beside thee”. What do the readings claim for bodily presence in a particular place, and what do they concede to Kabir?
Israel at Sinai and Isaiah in the temple are afraid of what the pilgrims in these readings travel months to find. Is the fear missing here, or changed into something else?
David is told “thou didst well that it was in thine heart”, and the reward of attaining is recorded for whoever desired it. What does this say about those who were prevented, and about us?
Jesus says it is expedient that he go away, and that those who have not seen are blessed. How do remembered presence and promised reunion change the meaning of absence?
Peter wished to stay on the mountain. Why does the guide end with thanks and service and not with the meeting itself?

outside.why: To attain the presence of the holy Luminaries is to attain the “Presence of God”. Jesus answers Philip’s request to be shown the Father in the same way: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Moses asks to see the glory and is told that no man shall see the face and live; he is shown only what passes by. Is meeting God through another a lesser thing, or the only meeting there is?
The reading’s Jacob scents Joseph’s garment from a thousand leagues. In Genesis the old man’s spirit revives at the mere report and the sight of the wagons: far off, he is already on his way.
“Thou art present and visible”, though far from the Shrine. Paul writes to a church he has not visited that he is absent in the flesh yet with them in the spirit, joying and beholding their order.
“Whenever thou rememberest thy merciful Lord, verily He is present before thy face.” The Qur’an makes the same promise in God’s own voice: when My servants question thee concerning Me, I am nigh.
“He knoweth thee in thy turning and thy resting-place.” The psalmist says it almost word for word: thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, and art acquainted with all my ways.
He who has attained “Thy presence hath attained unto the presence of God”. Paul locates the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in a face.
The life the Prophets speak of is “the life of knowledge”. John’s Gospel defines life eternal the same way: that they might know thee, and him whom thou hast sent.

The purpose of creating man is that he know his Creator and attain His presence. Augustine opens his Confessions on the same claim, put as an ache: made for Thee, the heart is restless till it rest in Thee.

The reading quotes this verse: Moses asks to look upon God and is told “Thou wilt not see Me”, and the mountain crumbles. The Qur’an’s story ends with Moses senseless; the reading says the veil is now rent.
“This is the Day in which mankind can behold the Face.” Jesus tells his disciples that many prophets and kings desired to see what they see, and did not see it.
The pastoral letter speaks of One dwelling in light which no man can approach, whom no man hath seen nor can see. What kind of beholding does the reading promise, if this still stands?
Blessed is whoever “entered Thy presence, and caught the accents of Thy voice” on the long-announced Day. Old Simeon, who had waited for it, takes the child in his arms and says his eyes have seen.
A day on which “all eyes can gaze upon the beauty of the All-Glorious”. The Apocalypse ends with the same promise held out for the city to come: they shall see his face.
“Where are the eyes worthy of this Day?” In John the coming of the light divides: those who see not are made to see, and those who say “We see” are found blind.
“The Spirit calleth aloud” with tidings of the presence of God. In the last chapter of the Bible the Spirit and the bride say, Come, and whoever is athirst may come.
A day of meeting, “yet most of the people are fast asleep”. Paul says the same to Rome: it is high time to awake out of sleep; the night is far spent.
The verses give tidings of “the meeting with their Lord”. The Qur’an’s own phrase is the source: whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work.
Meeting Him “was the hope of the chosen ones”. Job, from the ash-heap, holds to that hope with nothing to support it: yet in my flesh shall I see God, mine eyes shall behold.
“The thirsty one seeks the Kawthar of Thy presence.” The best-known image of that thirst is the psalmist’s hart panting after the water brooks: when shall I come and appear before God?
Tears, sighs and yearning to meet. The psalm from the wilderness of Judah has the same bodily longing: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land.
One who has “left his abode, turning toward Thy abode”. The pilgrim psalm envies even the sparrow that nests at the altar: my soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord.

Here the soul leaves home to seek. Francis Thompson tells the story the other way: “I fled Him, down the nights and down the days”, and it is God who pursues. Which is the truer account of how a meeting comes about?
The lover leaves home crying “Where art Thou?” morn and eve. The woman of the Song rises by night and goes about the streets seeking him whom her soul loveth.
The reading does not shrink from the language of lovers. Nor does the Song of Solomon, read for two thousand years as the soul’s love for God: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”

“Come thou and draw nigh.” Herbert’s soul, bidden welcome by Love, draws back “guilty of dust and sin”, and has to be told to sit and eat. What does the invitation ask of the one who feels unfit for it?
“The fire of thy separation from Me was fast consuming thee.” Rumi’s Mathnawi opens with that fire: the reed-flute complaining of its banishment from the reed-bed.
“Cast me not away from the gate of the city of Thy presence.” David’s psalm of repentance asks it in nearly the same words.
To roam before His presence and be seated “at the right hand of the throne”. Psalm 16 joins the same two things: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand, pleasures for evermore.
The prayer asks that attaining the presence be ordained. James turns the same hope into a counsel with a promise: draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.
The prayer recalls “the Call by which the ear of Thy Moses was privileged in the Sinai”. Exodus tells it: a bush that burned and was not consumed, and a voice calling him by name.
At the same mountain the people stand afar off and beg Moses: speak thou with us, but let not God speak with us, lest we die. The readings long for what Israel feared. What has changed, or who?

The suppliant asks to soar on wings of detachment to the heights. The psalmist finds that with the wings of the morning, in heaven or in the uttermost sea, the hand is already there. Is the ascent a journey or a recognition?
“That none may be seen except Thee.” The Qur’an says of everything on earth that it will pass away, and there remaineth but the countenance of thy Lord.
“I have turned my face toward the Dayspring of the lights of Thy countenance.” Unto God belong East and West, says the Qur’an: whithersoever ye turn, there is God’s countenance.

“Look upon them with the glances of Thy loving-kindness.” The priestly blessing of Israel asks the same in its oldest form: the Lord make his face shine upon thee, and lift up his countenance upon thee.
“Wilt Thou cast away this evanescent one?” The question has an answer in John’s Gospel: him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
“Write down for them” and number them with those who circle the throne. Jesus tells the seventy to rejoice less in their powers than in this, that their names are written in heaven.
“Cast away all that ye possess.” The merchant of the parable does exactly that when he has found one pearl of great price.
People are taught to “return to the homeland”. Hebrews says of the patriarchs that they confessed themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth, seeking a country of their own.
“The final homeland of the lovers.” Abraham in Hebrews leaves home looking for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
Nothing equals a moment before the Throne, “though one possessed all that is in the heavens and earth”. The psalmist: a day in thy courts is better than a thousand; I had rather be a doorkeeper.
Kabir’s God says: “O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee”, neither in temple nor in mosque. Against that, what does the reading claim for appearing “in the visible realm”?
Attaining the presence “is better for him than the worship of both humans and jinn”. Mary sits at Jesus’s feet while Martha serves, and is told she has chosen the good part.
“Thou didst enter the prison, and present thyself.” The Gospel knows another visit to a prison counted as a visit to its Lord: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. How far apart are the two visits?
He “didst purpose to reach the true Ka‘bih”. The Qur’an lays on those who can find a way the pilgrimage to the House where Abraham stood.
A traveller crosses sea and land to hear a voice. The queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth on a report, to prove Solomon with hard questions.
He traversed land and sea until he entered the Luminous Spot. The wise men of Matthew travel from the east after a star, asking where he is, for they have come to worship.

The pilgrim who died near his goal “raced in the arena of the love of God”. Chaucer’s pilgrims set out because it is April and folk long to go: he reminds us how mixed the motives of a pilgrimage can be, and how unlike this one.
He “crossed the deserts and wastes and valleys and seas”. The pilgrim psalm blesses those who pass through the valley of Baca and make it a well.
Hasan was present “in successive years … in all nights and days”. What the psalm hopes for in its last line, he is told he had: to dwell in the house of the Lord.
All were given to drink “from the ocean of Thy reunion and the springs of Thy nearness”. Psalm 36: thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures.
“Time after time and repeatedly” he came to the Court. Israel’s law made such returning a rhythm: three times in a year to appear before the Lord, and not empty.
“The Tongue of God spoke with thee openly.” Exodus says of Moses in the tent that the Lord spake unto him face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend.
“A single moment’s pause in the Desired Land cannot be equaled by centuries.” Blake’s couplet makes the same exchange of measures: infinity in the palm of the hand, eternity in an hour.
“Remember the days of meeting Me.” The two at Emmaus understand their meeting only in remembering it: did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?
Presence becomes memory. Jesus tells his friends that it is expedient for them that he go away, for otherwise the Comforter will not come. Can an absence complete what a presence began?
He “appeared before the Throne with evident humility”. Moses at the bush is told to draw not nigh and to put off his shoes, for the place is holy ground.

The pilgrim hears and witnesses, and is congratulated. Isaiah, seeing the Lord, cries “Woe is me! for I am undone”, a man of unclean lips. Where has that dread gone in these readings, or is it folded into the humility they mention?
He turned to Him “at a time when all mankind … have arisen to turn away”. When many disciples walk no more with Jesus, Peter answers for the few: Lord, to whom shall we go?
“Without veil or barrier” illumined by the light of the countenance. Paul: we all, with open face beholding the glory, are changed into the same image.
“She was honoured with attaining Thy presence in Thy days.” Mary Magdalene, weeping in the garden, is the first in John to see and to be called by name.
“Blessed art thou in that thou hast drawn nigh.” The same beatitude is spoken in Matthew over eyes and ears: blessed are your eyes, for they see.
To meet is called a mighty triumph. On the road to Emmaus two disciples walk beside the one they mourn and their eyes are holden. What besides being in the presence does a meeting need?
“Blessed is he who hath migrated.” Abraham is the first migrant of faith, who went out not knowing whither he went.
“Thou didst respond to thy Lord when He called thee.” The boy Samuel is taught the answer: Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth.
The believer is praised for hearing “with thine own ear”. Thomas is told that those who have not seen and yet have believed are blessed. Which blessing is the greater, and which is open to us?
He arrived, attained, and “became aware of His holy and sanctified Person”. The Samaritans say it plainly: now we believe, not because of thy saying, for we have heard him ourselves.

He attained “that for which thou wast created from nothingness into being”. The Westminster divines answer their first question the same way: man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever.
Javad “heard the Call and ran forward intoxicated”. At Pentecost the bystanders can only explain the disciples by saying that they are full of new wine.
“How many servants desired to attain the presence but were prevented.” Moses is shown the land from Nebo and told: thou shalt not go over thither.

“The smoke of heedless hearts hath become an obstacle.” Isaiah names the same barrier: your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and hid his face. Here, though, the barrier is other people’s hatred.
He “records for whosoever desires it the reward of attaining His presence”. Paul’s rule for gifts is the same rule: if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted.

The desire is counted as the journey made. Jesus says the kingdom comes not with observation, “lo here” or “lo there”: it is within you. Does that make the journey unnecessary, or explain why the desire can stand for it?
The reward is ordained for whoever “hath desired … to stand before His gate”. David, forbidden to build the temple, is told: thou didst well that it was in thine heart.
“He who desires My presence is among those who have attained.” Pascal hears Christ say: Console thyself, thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me.
“We ordain for whomsoever We please the reward.” The householder pays the last hired as the first and asks: is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own?
God ordains the reward “for whomsoever He wishes”. At Sinai the Lord says: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious.
A woman “turned to the Countenance … when most men turned away”. Ruth turns when her sister-in-law goes back: whither thou goest, I will go; thy God shall be my God.
“Wert thou to be present before the Throne and hear it…” The officers sent to arrest Jesus come back empty-handed: never man spake like this man.

Revelation educates men to ascend at death “in the utmost purity and sanctity”. Socrates, on his last day, argues that the soul which has kept itself pure departs to what is like itself, the divine and immortal.
He “attained the meeting of his Lord”. The Qur’an’s address to the dying: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure; enter among My bondmen.
He hastened away “crying ‘My Lord, receive me!’” Stephen, the first Christian martyr, dies with the same cry.
“Permit him … to behold Thy beauty.” Psalm 17: I will behold thy face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.
“He desired to ascend to the canopy of union.” Paul in prison is torn the same way: a desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better, and the need to stay.
“When the doors of the Kingdom are opened … seek thou reunion with Him instantly.” Paul: willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.

The Preacher looks at the same door and sees nothing behind it: the dead know not any thing, and have no more a portion in what is done under the sun. Everything in these readings rests on his being wrong; on what do they rest it?
Strive “that at the time of ascension ye may meet the luminous countenance”. John’s letter: it doth not yet appear what we shall be, but we shall see him as he is.
One who “ever lived thirsting for the cup of meeting Thee”. Tennyson, old, asks for no moaning of the bar: “I hope to see my Pilot face to face.”
“Tomorrow night we shall be the guests of God.” The same calm certainty is given to the thief on the cross: To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
“Praise be to Thee … for raising me up on this Promised Day.” The psalm’s shout: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
The reading echoes John’s vision nearly word for word: the holy city, the tabernacle of God with men, “and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people”.
“An eternal celebration”, the brimming cup. Isaiah foresees a feast made for all peoples on the mountain, where the veil spread over the nations is destroyed.

The glad tidings is a friend’s coming, and the hope of “attainment unto His presence”. The elder ends a letter the same way: not with ink and pen; I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face.
Meeting, “the greatest of God’s bounties”, is here a meeting of friends under one Tree. The psalm of ascents: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
“Praise be unto Thee … for having given me to drink.” The psalmist asks what he shall render for all the benefits, and answers: I will take the cup of salvation.
“Having remembered me from Thy most exalted horizon.” Psalm 8 wonders at being remembered at all, and at the dignity conferred with it.
He spoke “that which I am unable to mention except according to my weakness”. Paul, caught up to paradise, heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
“A station which meanings cannot reach, nor utterance.” Dante’s poem ends where his high fantasy fails, his desire and will turned by the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.
Peter on the mountain wants to build three tabernacles and stay. They go down again. The guide’s arc ends with service as the fruit of meeting; what would be lost if the pilgrim never went home?
